goal: Vercel's one cron calls a small watcher every 15 minutes that emails the platform's admins when the scheduler has stopped, the daily job is scheduled once (by pg_cron only), pg_cron's own SQL jobs each have a ledger row, and the status page's jobs check fails on a late watcher or a late daily job.
why: The daily route is scheduled twice at 07:00 UTC, by pg_cron and by Vercel's cron, so about 40 functions can run twice at once; and if pg_cron stops, nothing runs and nothing says so, because every check runs from the scheduler itself. After this step commerce.cron_jobs.runs for route.subscription-reminders rises by exactly 1 a day and a stopped scheduler is told by email within 30 minutes.

commits.title: pg_cron's own SQL jobs get a ledger row each, checked daily

changes.how: Server-only. Export checkPgCronJobs(): Promise<{ jobs: number; failed: string[] }>. First: select to_regclass('cron.job') is not null as present; when false (a local database without pg_cron) return { jobs: 0, failed: [] }. Then read pg_cron's SQL jobs: select jobid, jobname from cron.job where command not ilike '%net.http_post%' and jobname like 'kaizen-%' (the jobs that call a route have ledger rows of their own already). For each, read its newest run: select status, end_time from cron.job_run_details where jobid = $1 order by start_time desc limit 1. Record each job in the ledger with tracked(`pgcron.${jobname}`, 86_400, async () => { if (!run) throw new Error('no run recorded'); if (run.status === 'failed') throw new Error('last run failed'); }) from './cron-runs' (tracked() writes the row, counts a failure and returns null when the function throws). Then one more ledger row for the log itself: tracked('pgcron.run-log', 86_400, async () => { const oldest = select min(end_time) from cron.job_run_details; if (oldest is older than 8 days) throw new Error('the oldest row of cron.job_run_details is over 8 days old: its prune is not running'); }). Return the count and the names whose tracked() answered null. Read through typedRows() with zod rows. The job names are lower case with hyphens, which the ledger's key rule accepts ('^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9_.:-]{0,63}$'); skip and log a name that does not fit.

In run(), directly after the line that runs tracked("daily.database-door", ...), add: const pgCron = await checkPgCronJobs().catch((error) => (log('error', 'pg_cron_jobs.check_failed', {}, error), { jobs: 0, failed: [] })); and add pgCronJobs: pgCron.jobs and pgCronFailed: pgCron.failed.length to the JSON answer. Import log from '@/server/log' if the file does not import it.

CI's and local databases may have no pg_cron. Case 1 (always): when to_regclass('cron.job') is null, checkPgCronJobs() returns { jobs: 0, failed: [] } and throws nothing. Case 2 (only when the cron schema is absent, so the test may create a stand-in; skip with a printed reason when the real extension is there): create schema cron with two tables shaped as pg_cron's (cron.job(jobid bigint, jobname text, command text) and cron.job_run_details(jobid bigint, status text, start_time timestamptz, end_time timestamptz)); insert the SQL job 'kaizen-consent-retention' with a succeeded run an hour ago, 'kaizen-cookie-scan-retention' with a failed run, and a route job whose command holds net.http_post; run checkPgCronJobs(): commerce.cron_jobs has rows pgcron.kaizen-consent-retention (failures 0), pgcron.kaizen-cookie-scan-retention (failures 1) and pgcron.run-log, and no row for the route job; then insert a run that ended 9 days ago and run again: pgcron.run-log's failures rose. Drop the stand-in schema and delete the pgcron.% ledger rows in afterAll.
